title: In Re: Judge Mark B. Cohen
description: Whether a sitting judge's First Amendment right to free speech protects their partisan commentary and "tout[ing]" of past legislative deeds from disciplinary action under the Code of Judicial Conduct.
plaintiff_argument: Judge Cohen argued that his speech, including partisan commentary and referencing past legislative actions, is protected by his First Amendment rights and does not inherently violate judicial conduct rules.
defendant_argument: The Court of Judicial Discipline/Judicial Conduct Board argued that Judge Cohen's "avidly and insistently partisan tilt" and "tout[ing]" of legislative deeds transgressed the Code of Judicial Conduct, as judges must curtail some free speech rights to maintain impartiality.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the order of the Court of Judicial Discipline, ruling that Judge Mark B. Cohen's partisan commentary and "tout[ing]" of legislative deeds, in context, violated judicial conduct rules, thereby limiting a sitting judge's free speech rights.

title: Commonwealth v. Kurtz
description: Whether there was sufficient evidence of probable cause to support the issuance of the warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that there was sufficient probable cause to support the issuance of the warrant.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that there was insufficient probable cause to support the issuance of the warrant.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of sentence, finding that there was sufficient probable cause to support the warrant.

title: Rivera v. Borough of Pottstown
description: Whether the Borough's Code provisions authorizing administrative warrants for biennial rental inspections on less than individualized probable cause are facially constitutional under Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Borough's Code provisions allowing administrative search warrants for rental inspections without individualized probable cause violate their privacy rights and freedom from unreasonable searches under the Pennsylvania Constitution.
defendant_argument: The Borough's Code provisions are valid, do not violate constitutional rights, and individualized probable cause is not required for administrative warrants for rental inspections.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Borough's Code provisions authorizing administrative warrants for biennial rental inspections on less than individualized probable cause are facially unconstitutional and enjoined the Borough from conducting such inspections.

title: Chilutti v. Uber
description: Whether a trial court order granting a petition to compel arbitration of ongoing litigation constitutes an immediately appealable collateral order under Pennsylvania Rule of Appellate Procedure 313.
plaintiff_argument: The Chiluttis argued that the trial court's order compelling arbitration was an immediately appealable collateral order because postponing review until final judgment would result in the irreparable loss of their claims, and they contended there was no valid agreement to arbitrate.
defendant_argument: Uber argued that the trial court's order compelling arbitration was not an immediately appealable collateral order because the issue could be reviewed on appeal after a final judgment, and the limited standard of review for common law arbitration awards does not apply to trial court orders compelling arbitration.
decision_outcome: The court held that the trial court's order compelling arbitration and staying court proceedings does not qualify as a collateral order, vacating the Superior Court's judgment and remanding the case with instructions to quash the appeal.

title: Commonwealth v. Hunte
description: Whether Section 3755 of the Vehicle Code, which authorizes warrantless blood draws based on probable cause in certain motor vehicle accident cases, violates the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that Section 3755 is constitutional, asserting that warrantless blood draws are permissible if a warrant is obtained later or if exigent circumstances justify the draw, and that the troopers complied with the law.
defendant_argument: Hunte argued that Section 3755 is unconstitutional because it facially authorizes warrantless blood draws based solely on probable cause, without a warrant or a recognized exception, and that implied consent or exigent circumstances do not justify such a categorical rule.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, declaring Section 3755 of the Vehicle Code unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, and dismissing related charges.

title: Department of Environmental Protection v. Pennsylvania Legislative Reference Bureau; Bowfin KeyCon Holdings v. Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection
description: Whether environmental nonprofit organizations should be permitted to intervene in litigation challenging the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) Regulation, and whether the appeal from the preliminary injunction of the RGGI Regulation is moot.
plaintiff_argument: The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) argued that the RGGI Regulation should be deemed approved and published, and that the Nonprofits' interests were adequately represented by DEP, making their intervention unnecessary.
defendant_argument: The Pennsylvania Legislative Reference Bureau (LRB) and legislative members (Senators and Representatives) argued that the RGGI Regulation was unlawful (e.g., an unconstitutional tax, exceeding DEP's authority), and that Nonprofits' interests were already adequately represented by DEP, thus denying intervention was proper.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Commonwealth Court's denial of intervention for the Nonprofits, allowing them to participate in the ongoing litigation, and dismissed the appeal from the preliminary injunction as moot due to the issuance of a permanent injunction.

title: Commonwealth v. Anthony Lewis
description: Whether police had reasonable suspicion to pursue Anthony Lewis, leading to the seizure of a firearm, based on his presence in a "high-crime area," proximity to alleged gambling, and flight, thereby justifying the denial of his motion to suppress evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that reasonable suspicion was established by the combination of the area being a high-crime area, Lewis being with a group appearing to gamble, and his flight from police.
defendant_argument: Anthony Lewis argued that he was unlawfully seized when police pursued him without reasonable suspicion, making his abandonment of the firearm coerced and subject to suppression.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, which denied Anthony Lewis's motion to suppress the firearm, finding that reasonable suspicion for the seizure existed.

title: Ferguson v. Department of Transportation
description: Whether treating participation in an Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition (ARD) program as a "prior offense" for purposes of suspending a driver's license upon a subsequent DUI conviction violates the Pennsylvania Constitution's due process principles.
plaintiff_argument: Ferguson argued that using ARD participation as a "prior offense" for license suspension is fundamentally unfair and a due process violation because ARD does not involve an admission of guilt or a formal conviction, thus lacking a logical basis to deprive him of his driver's license.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth (PennDOT) argued that treating ARD as a "prior offense" for license suspension is a constitutional exercise of legislative power, rationally related to the legitimate goal of promoting public safety on roadways by regulating motorists who pose a danger.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that treating ARD as a "prior offense" for driver's license suspension does not violate the Pennsylvania Constitution.

title: Center for Coalfield Justice v. Washington County Board of Elections
description: Whether county election boards are required to implement "notice and cure" procedures for defective mail ballots and allow provisional voting, or if such procedures are not statutorily mandated and lead to non-uniform elections.
plaintiff_argument: County election boards must provide notice to voters with defective mail ballots and offer an opportunity to cure or cast a provisional ballot, as implied by the Election Code and prior rulings.
defendant_argument: County election boards are not statutorily required to implement "notice and cure" procedures for defective mail ballots, and doing so without legislative authority creates non-uniform elections.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that county election boards must provide notice and an opportunity to cure defects in mail ballots or allow provisional voting, broadening the application of previous rulings.

title: Firearms Owners Against Crime v. Commissioner of Pennsylvania State Police
description: Whether the Pennsylvania State Police (PSP) is fulfilling its statutory obligation to perform "instantaneous" and "immediate" background checks for firearm purchases, and what forms of relief are available for alleged delays.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, FOAC, argued that PSP's understaffing of the PICS Operations Section caused significant delays in background checks, violating the Uniform Firearms Act's requirements for "instantaneous" and "immediate" responses, leading to lost sales and prejudicing firearm purchasers. They sought injunctive relief, mandamus, declaratory relief, and a refund for fees on cancelled transactions due to delays.
defendant_argument: The defendant, PSP, contended that "instantaneous" refers to the automated database search, while "immediate" or "forthwith" for human-involved checks allows for a "reasonable time" to ensure public safety by preventing firearms from going to prohibited persons. PSP argued staffing decisions are discretionary and budgetary, thus not subject to mandamus or injunctive relief, and that the $2.00 fee is non-refundable as costs are incurred regardless of transaction completion.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of injunctive and mandamus relief and the dissolution of the preliminary injunction, but reversed the denial of declaratory relief and vacated the order denying leave to amend, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: In re Prospect Crozer LLC
description: Whether a judicial officer's simultaneous holding of a judicial office and a compensated government board position violates the Pennsylvania Constitution's Article V, Section 17(a), and if so, what the appropriate remedy is for orders issued under such circumstances.
plaintiff_argument: Prospect argued that Judge Braxton held incompatible offices in violation of Article V, Section 17(a) of the Pennsylvania Constitution, leading to the forfeiture of his judicial office and rendering his orders legal nullities, thus requiring new adjudications.
defendant_argument: The District argued that Prospect's application to vacate was untimely, that only the Judicial Conduct Board and Court of Judicial Discipline have authority to address Section 17 violations, and that Judge Braxton's status as a "part-time" senior judge removed him from the purview of cases concerning incompatible offices.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order to vacate the trial court's orders and remand the cases for reassignment to a new judge, but on the alternative basis that Judge Braxton's simultaneous holding of incompatible offices created a voidable conflict of duties, not an automatic forfeiture of office or non-waivable structural error.

title: Crawford v. Commonwealth
description: Whether state firearm preemption laws (FPLs) violate the Pennsylvania Constitution by infringing on citizens' rights to life and liberty, creating a state-created danger, or improperly interfering with Philadelphia's delegated public health duties, thereby preventing local governments from enacting their own gun control ordinances.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that state firearm preemption laws (FPLs) are unconstitutional because they violate citizens' substantive due process rights to life and liberty, create a state-created danger by preventing local gun control, and improperly interfere with Philadelphia's delegated public health duties to address gun violence. They believe local governments should be allowed to enact gun safety measures to reduce gun violence.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the FPLs are constitutional and do not violate any rights. They contend that the Pennsylvania Constitution protects individuals from state action, not private violence, and does not grant a collective right to self-defense through local legislation. They also assert that the state-created danger doctrine is not applicable to invalidate statutes and that public health laws do not delegate authority to local governments to regulate firearms.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, dismissing the Petition with prejudice, ruling that the plaintiffs failed to state a legally cognizable claim that the firearm preemption laws are unconstitutional or otherwise infirm.

title: In re The Thirtieth County Investigating Grand Jury
description: Whether an investigating grand jury report met the statutory definition for public release and whether all named, non-indicted individuals criticized in such a report are entitled to due process notice and an opportunity to be heard.
plaintiff_argument: The Petitioner argued that the grand jury report did not meet the statutory definition for public release and that all named, non-indicted individuals criticized in the report are entitled to due process notice and an opportunity to be heard.
defendant_argument: The DAO argued that the grand jury report satisfied the statutory definition for public release and that the supervising judge had discretion in providing notice and opportunity to respond to criticized individuals.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the supervising judge's order to unseal the report, ruling that the report did not meet the statutory definition for public release, and remanded with instructions to permanently seal it, further determining that all named but nonindicted individuals criticized in a grand jury report must be given notice and an opportunity to respond.

title: Genser v. Butler County Board of Elections
description: Whether provisional ballots cast by electors whose mail-in ballots were rejected due to a missing secrecy envelope should be counted, or if such counting constitutes an improper court-mandated curing procedure contrary to the Election Code.
plaintiff_argument: The electors argued that their void mail-in ballots were legal nullities and did not constitute 'casting a ballot,' therefore their provisional ballots should be counted to prevent disenfranchisement and uphold their right to vote.
defendant_argument: The Republican Party argued that counting provisional ballots after a defective mail-in ballot was timely received would be an improper court-mandated curing procedure, contrary to the Election Code and prior precedent, as the voter had already 'cast' a ballot.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, directing the Butler County Board of Elections to count the electors' provisional ballots.

title: Commonwealth v. Yard
description: Whether the "proof is evident or presumption great" evidentiary standard applies to the life-imprisonment exception for denying bail under Article I, Section 14 of the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the "proof is evident or presumption great" standard does not apply to the life-imprisonment exception, meaning bail can be denied simply by being charged with an offense carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.
defendant_argument: Michael Noel Yard argued that the "proof is evident or presumption great" standard does apply to the life-imprisonment exception, and the Commonwealth had not met that burden for first-degree murder, also citing the plain English statement for the 1998 amendment.
decision_outcome: The court held that the "proof/presumption limitation" does not apply to the life-offense exception to the right to bail under the Pennsylvania Constitution, meaning defendants charged with offenses carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment are categorically precluded from release on bail. The lower court's order granting nominal bail was vacated and the matter remanded.

title: Krasner v. Ward
description: Whether Articles of Impeachment passed by one session of the General Assembly carry over into a subsequent legislative assembly after the previous session adjourned sine die, with the plaintiff arguing they do not and the defendant arguing they do.
plaintiff_argument: The Articles of Impeachment, as pending business, became null and void upon the sine die adjournment of the 206th General Assembly on November 30, 2022, and therefore cannot carry over to the 207th General Assembly.
defendant_argument: The Articles of Impeachment and related legislative business are not terminated by the sine die adjournment of a General Assembly session and can carry over to a new session, as impeachment is a judicial power distinct from legislative functions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's decision, holding that the Articles of Impeachment passed by the 206th Session of the General Assembly became null and void upon its expiration on November 30, 2022.

title: Oberholzer v. Galapo
description: Whether an injunction prohibiting ongoing publication of signs on one's own property constitutes an impermissible prior restraint on speech under Article I, Section 7 of the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Oberholzers argued that the Galapos' signs constituted targeted picketing and expressive conduct designed to inflict psychological harm and invade their residential privacy, thus justifying an injunction as a permissible time, place, and manner restriction, not an unconstitutional prior restraint, and that their right to quiet enjoyment of their home outweighed the Galapos' speech rights.
defendant_argument: The Galapos argued that their signs constituted pure speech, protected by Article I, Section 7 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, and that the injunction against them was an impermissible prior restraint on speech, regardless of whether the underlying tort claims were for defamation, false light, nuisance, or other speech-related torts.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Superior Court's order vacating the injunction entered by the trial court and ordered the injunction dissolved.

title: Commonwealth v. Thompson
description: Whether inventory searches remain valid under Pennsylvania's Constitution following the rejection of the federal automobile exception to the warrant requirement.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Appellant Michael Thompson) argues that inventory searches are unconstitutional under Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, especially in light of Commonwealth v. Alexander's rejection of the diminished-privacy rationale for vehicles.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Commonwealth of Pennsylvania) argues that inventory searches remain valid under Pennsylvania law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania dismissed the appeal as improvidently granted, thereby upholding the lower court's decision that affirmed the judgment of sentence.

title: Commonwealth v. Torsilieri
description: Whether the General Assembly's determination that sexual offenders pose a high risk of committing additional sexual offenses constitutes an unconstitutional irrebuttable presumption violative of due process, and whether the registration and notification requirements in Subchapter H of SORNA constitute criminal punishment.
plaintiff_argument: Appellee argued that SORNA's irrebuttable presumption that sex offenders pose a high risk of reoffending is unconstitutional, violating due process and the right to reputation, and that its registration and notification requirements constitute criminal punishment, violating separation of powers and cruel and unusual punishment prohibitions.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth argued that SORNA's presumption is valid, as Appellee failed to demonstrate a scientific consensus refuting it, and that the registration and notification requirements are not punitive but serve the non-punitive purpose of public protection through information sharing.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's order, finding that Appellee failed to prove SORNA's irrebuttable presumption unconstitutional and that Subchapter H's registration and notification requirements do not constitute criminal punishment.

title: City of Lancaster v. Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission
description: Whether Section 59.18 of the PUC's regulations, which grants natural gas distribution companies (NGDCs) discretion over gas meter placement in historic districts, constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The Municipalities argued that Section 59.18 unlawfully delegates unfettered legislative authority to NGDCs to determine gas meter locations in historic districts without adequate standards or review, violating the Pennsylvania Constitution.
defendant_argument: The PUC contended that Section 59.18 does not grant absolute discretion to NGDCs, requires consideration of inside meter placement in historic districts, allows for PUC review, and that the General Assembly never vested the PUC with legislative authority over meter location in historic districts, thus no delegation occurred.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, concluding that the General Assembly never enacted a statute vesting the PUC with legislative authority over gas meter locations in historic districts, meaning there was no legislative authority to delegate.

title: Scott v. Pennsylvania Board of Parole
description: Whether the Commonwealth Court has original jurisdiction to hear claims challenging the constitutionality of a statute that renders individuals sentenced to life imprisonment ineligible for parole, or if such claims are in the nature of post-conviction relief and thus outside its jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Commonwealth Court had original jurisdiction because they were not challenging their life imprisonment sentences but rather their parole eligibility, which they contended was a separate matter, and that depriving them of parole opportunities violated state and federal constitutions.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Commonwealth Court lacked jurisdiction because the plaintiffs' claims were in the nature of applications for post-conviction relief, which is statutorily excluded from the Commonwealth Court's original jurisdiction, and that parole eligibility is integral to the criminal sentence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's holding that it lacked jurisdiction over the appellants' petition, concluding that the claims fundamentally challenged the constitutionality of their sentences and thus fell under post-conviction relief.

title: Siger v. City of Chester
description: Whether the Act 47 receiver for a financially distressed municipality has the authority to implement a recovery plan that suspends local elected officials' administrative duties, controls legislative agenda items, and waives residency requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The Receiver argued that the modifications to the recovery plan were necessary to achieve financial stability for the distressed municipality, given the local officials' lack of cooperation and mismanagement, and that Act 47 grants broad powers to implement the recovery plan.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the Receiver's proposed modifications unlawfully deprived its elected officials of their authority, impermissibly altered the City's form of government, were not necessary for financial stability, and that requiring the City Solicitor to disclose privileged information was improper.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania affirmed the order of the Commonwealth Court, upholding the Receiver's proposed modifications to the recovery plan.

title: Weeks v. Department of Human Service of the Commonwealth
description: Whether Act 12 of 2019 violated Article III, Sections 1 and 3 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it changed its original purpose, had a deceptive title, and covered multiple subjects, and the defendant arguing it satisfied all constitutional requirements as its purpose remained broad and its provisions were germane to a single subject.
plaintiff_argument: Appellants argued that Act 12 violated Article III, Sections 1 and 3 of the Pennsylvania Constitution because its original purpose changed, its title was deceptive, and its provisions covered more than a single subject, specifically by combining disparate subjects like eliminating Cash Assistance with revenue-raising measures for hospitals and public health programs.
defendant_argument: Appellee argued that Act 12 did not violate Article III, Sections 1 and 3 because the original and final bill related to the same broad purpose of "benefits pertaining to the basic necessities of life to low-income individuals," the title was not deceptive, and all amendments were germane to this single subject.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the order of the Commonwealth Court, ruling that Act 12 was constitutional and that the legislative process satisfied Article III's requirements.

title: The Marcellus Shale Coalition v. Department of Environmental Protection of the Commonwealth
description: Whether the Department of Environmental Protection and the Environmental Quality Board exceeded their legislative rulemaking authority by defining "other critical communities," "common areas of a school's property," "playground," and including "playground owners" and "municipalities" as "public resource agencies" in regulations for unconventional gas wells.
plaintiff_argument: The Marcellus Shale Coalition (MSC) argued that the Agencies exceeded their statutory authority by promulgating these regulations, which are unlawful, illegal, void, and unenforceable, and create a new pre-permitting scheme without statutory authority. They contended the definitions are not of the same general nature or class as statutory items and that the PNDI process violates the Documents Law.
defendant_argument: The Agencies argued that the General Assembly intended to give them broad leeway to promulgate the challenged regulations, which are reasonable and fall within their statutory authority, especially considering their constitutional duties under the Environmental Rights Amendment. They contended the Commonwealth Court misapplied agency law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, finding that the Agencies did not exceed their legislative rulemaking powers in enacting the challenged regulations.

title: GM Berkshire Hills LLC v. Berks County Board of Assessment
description: Whether a school district's method of selectively appealing property assessments, based on a cost-benefit threshold and the Common Level Ratio, violates the Uniformity Clause of the Pennsylvania Constitution by creating discriminatory results.
plaintiff_argument: The school district's method for selecting properties for reassessment is discriminatory and violates the Uniformity Clause, leading to an unfair and disproportionately increased tax burden on their property.
defendant_argument: The school district's method for selecting properties for reassessment is neutral, enhances uniformity by targeting non-uniform properties, and does not violate the Uniformity Clause, especially when applying the Common Level Ratio.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's decision, ruling that the school district's selective property assessment appeal method violates the Uniformity Clause.

title: McLinko v. Commonwealth
description: Whether Act 77, which allows for universal mail-in voting, violates the Pennsylvania Constitution by expanding voting methods beyond constitutionally permitted exceptions for in-person voting.
plaintiff_argument: The Pennsylvania Constitution requires in-person voting, with limited exceptions for absentee voting, and Act 77 unconstitutionally expands mail-in voting beyond these exceptions.
defendant_argument: The General Assembly has broad authority under the Constitution to prescribe methods of voting, and Act 77's universal mail-in provisions do not violate any constitutional restrictions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, finding no constitutional violation in Act 77's universal mail-in voting provisions.

title: Pennsylvania Environmental Defense Foundation v. Commonwealth
description: Whether the Commonwealth's use of funds derived from oil and gas leases on state lands, and related legislative changes, violate the Environmental Rights Amendment by not solely serving trust purposes.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth's use of oil and gas lease proceeds for DCNR's general operations, allocation to projects outside the Marcellus Shale region, the repeal of the Oil and Gas Lease Fund Act, transfer of control to the General Assembly, commingling of funds, and transfer of Keystone Fund monies to the General Fund violate the Environmental Rights Amendment and the Commonwealth's trustee duties.
defendant_argument: The challenged uses of funds and legislative changes are consistent with the Environmental Rights Amendment and the Commonwealth's trustee duties, as DCNR's operations are necessary for conservation, there are no geographic restrictions on fund use, the Lease Fund remains a special fund with explicit trustee duty considerations, separate accounts are not mandated, and the Keystone Fund does not involve trust assets.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, concluding that PEDF failed to demonstrate that the challenged provisions violate the Pennsylvania Constitution, thereby ruling against PEDF on all its claims.

title: Commonwealth v. Jones-Williams
description: Whether the warrantless seizure of blood, already drawn and preserved by hospital personnel, was constitutional under the Fourth Amendment, specifically regarding the applicability of the exigent circumstances exception or the implied consent statute (75 Pa.C.S. § 3755).
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the warrantless blood test was constitutional because exigent circumstances existed due to the accident and Appellee's condition, and/or because the implied consent statute (Section 3755) authorized the seizure.
defendant_argument: Jones-Williams argued that the blood seizure was illegal because police lacked a warrant, and neither the exigent circumstances exception nor Section 3755 applied, as the blood evidence was preserved and a warrant could have been obtained.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Superior Court's decision to suppress the blood test results and remand for a new trial, but vacated the Superior Court's holding that Section 3755 was unconstitutional, deeming that constitutional question unnecessary to address.

title: Khalil v. Williams
description: Whether legal malpractice claims against attorneys following a settlement are barred by the Muhammad rule, or if exceptions apply when the claims are based on incorrect legal advice rather than the settlement amount, or on fraud.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that her legal malpractice claims were not barred by the Muhammad rule because they were based on her attorneys' erroneous legal advice regarding the scope and effect of a settlement release, which precluded her counterclaims in a separate case, and not merely on dissatisfaction with the settlement amount. She also alleged fraud, claiming the release she signed was switched.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiff's claims were barred by the Muhammad rule because her true objective was to revisit the settlement amount, and her fraud allegations had been previously rejected. They contended the case was distinguishable from precedents that allowed claims based on incorrect advice on well-established principles of law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed in part and affirmed in part the Superior Court's decision, holding that certain of the plaintiff's claims (negligence and breach of contract based on incorrect legal advice) are not barred by Muhammad, and her fraud claim can proceed, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Commonwealth v. Edwards
description: Whether a prosecutor's intentional racial discrimination during jury selection, in violation of Batson v. Kentucky, constitutes prosecutorial overreaching sufficient to preclude retrial on double jeopardy grounds under the Pennsylvania Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Derrick Edwards, argued that the prosecutor's intentional racial discrimination in jury selection (a Batson violation) was egregious prosecutorial misconduct that deprived him of a fair trial and subverted the truth-determining process, thus barring retrial under double jeopardy principles.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, argued that while a Batson violation warrants a new trial, it does not constitute the 'overwhelming and egregious' misconduct or 'deliberate, bad faith' intent required to preclude retrial on double jeopardy grounds, especially since the prosecutor's actions were not intended to provoke a mistrial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Superior Court, which affirmed the trial court's order denying the Appellant's motion to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds, thereby allowing retrial.

title: Commonwealth v. Barr
description: Whether the smell of marijuana alone can establish probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search, given the legalization of medical marijuana.
plaintiff_argument: The smell of marijuana alone should not establish probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search because medical marijuana is legal, and the Hicks decision dictates that lawful possession of an item cannot alone suggest criminal activity.
defendant_argument: The smell of marijuana remains a relevant factor for probable cause in a warrantless vehicle search, as the Medical Marijuana Act (MMA) only provides a limited exception to the general illegality of marijuana, and Hicks is distinguishable.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Superior Court's judgment, reinstated the trial court's order granting the Appellant's motion to suppress, and remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion, ruling that the odor of marijuana alone does not amount to probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search.

title: In re Interest of Y.W.-B.
description: Whether the Department of Human Services (DHS) established sufficient probable cause to compel a home inspection, and whether the Superior Court's standard for probable cause in child protective services cases violates Fourth Amendment and state constitutional protections against unreasonable searches.
plaintiff_argument: The Mother (plaintiff) argued that the Superior Court's decision created an unconstitutionally diluted probable cause standard for child welfare agencies, violating Fourth Amendment and state constitutional protections by eliminating particularity, reliability, and nexus requirements for home inspections.
defendant_argument: The Department of Human Services (DHS) (defendant) argued that a less stringent probable cause standard is appropriate for child protective services home inspections compared to criminal investigations, and that probable cause was established based on the totality of circumstances.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania reversed the Superior Court's order, concluding that DHS did not establish sufficient probable cause to compel a home inspection, thereby violating Mother's constitutional rights.

title: Commonwealth v. Talley
description: Whether the Commonwealth is required to produce clear and convincing evidence at a bail revocation hearing to deny bail based on public safety, and whether the Best Evidence Rule permits the introduction of text message screenshots that omit metadata.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the standard of proof for denying bail is a 'prima facie case' and that the affidavit of probable cause was sufficient. They also contended that the text message screenshots were admissible as originals or duplicates, and Talley's challenge was an authentication issue, not a best-evidence rule violation.
defendant_argument: Talley argued that the standard of proof for denying bail requires 'clear and convincing evidence' and that the Commonwealth failed to meet this burden. He also asserted that the text message screenshots were inadmissible under the Best Evidence Rule because they lacked metadata and did not accurately reproduce the original messages.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Superior Court's judgment, ruling that while the trial court erred in denying bail without an evidentiary hearing, Talley failed to prove prejudice, and that text message screenshots were admissible duplicates under the best-evidence rule.

title: League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania v. Degraffenreid
description: Whether the proposed Victim's Rights Amendment, presented as a single ballot question, violated Article XI, Section 1 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, which requires that multiple amendments be voted upon separately.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed Victim's Rights Amendment violates the separate vote requirement of Article XI, Section 1 because it contains multiple, distinct, and non-interrelated changes that substantively affect various existing constitutional provisions, thereby denying voters the right to approve or disapprove each change individually.
defendant_argument: The Victim's Rights Amendment is sufficiently interrelated and serves the common purpose of enshrining victims' rights, and it does not explicitly alter the language of other constitutional provisions, thus complying with the "separate vote" requirement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, declaring the proposed Victim's Rights Amendment unconstitutional for violating the separate vote requirement and permanently enjoining the Secretary of the Commonwealth from tabulating or certifying the election results.

title: Brooks v. Ewing Cole, Inc.
description: Whether an order denying a summary judgment motion based on sovereign immunity is an immediately appealable collateral order under Pennsylvania Rule of Appellate Procedure 313.
plaintiff_argument: Brooks argued that the Commonwealth Court correctly denied the interlocutory appeal because the order denying summary judgment was not a collateral order, as sovereign immunity is not irreparably lost if appellate review is postponed until final judgment.
defendant_argument: The Family Court argued that the order denying summary judgment on sovereign immunity is a collateral order and thus immediately appealable, because sovereign immunity protects government entities from suit, and this protection is irreparably lost if appellate review is postponed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court's order, concluding that the denial of summary judgment on sovereign immunity grounds is an appealable collateral order, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Pennsylvania Environmental Defense Foundation v. Commonwealth
description: Whether revenues from oil and gas leases on state lands, specifically bonus payments, rental fees, and interest penalties, constitute trust assets that must be returned to the trust corpus or if they are income that can be diverted to the General Fund.
plaintiff_argument: The PEDF argued that all revenues (bonus, rental, interest penalties) are inextricably linked to the sale of trust assets and must be returned to the trust corpus as principal, and that the ERA does not create income entitlements for beneficiaries.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth argued that bonus and rent payments are for an inchoate leasehold interest, not the sale of minerals, and thus are income that can be diverted, aligning with the 1947 Act's provisions for income distribution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Commonwealth Court, holding that while bonus payments, rentals, and late fees are income, the Environmental Rights Amendment (ERA) does not create income entitlements for beneficiaries, and therefore these revenues must be returned to the trust corpus for conservation and maintenance.

title: Commonwealth v. Eid
description: Whether the sentencing provision in 75 Pa.C.S. § 1543(b)(1.1)(i) is unconstitutionally vague because it fails to provide a clear statutory maximum penalty for refusing chemical testing after driving under a suspended license, violating state and federal due process principles.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the DUS statute is not unconstitutionally vague and a maximum term of six months can be reasonably inferred by reading it in conjunction with other sections of the Vehicle Code and historical legislative intent.
defendant_argument: Khalid Eid argued that the sentencing statute is unconstitutionally vague because it lacks an express maximum penalty, thereby violating due process by failing to provide fair notice of the consequences of one's actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Eid's conviction for refusing chemical testing but vacated his sentence of imprisonment, ruling that the sentencing statute was unconstitutionally vague due to the absence of a specified maximum term, and affirmed the mandatory $1,000 fine.

title: Commonwealth v. Hairston
description: Whether the death penalty is unconstitutional under the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I, Section 13 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, and whether trial and appellate counsel provided ineffective assistance.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the death penalty is constitutional, the verdict slip was valid, the prosecutor's arguments were proper, and that counsel was effective in all challenged aspects.
defendant_argument: Hairston argued that the death penalty is unconstitutional both facially and as-applied, and that his trial and appellate counsel were ineffective for failing to challenge the verdict slip, allowing prosecutorial misconduct, and allowing improper expert testimony.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the PCRA court's order denying relief, upholding Kenneth Hairston's death sentence and rejecting his claims of unconstitutionality and ineffective assistance of counsel.

title: Commonwealth v. Middaugh
description: Whether a driver's operating privileges can be suspended after an unreasonable delay between conviction and notification, particularly when the delay is not attributable to PennDOT, thereby denying the driver due process.
plaintiff_argument: The suspension of driving privileges is invalid due to the lengthy 28-month delay between his DUI conviction and PennDOT's notification, which caused him significant prejudice and violated his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The suspension should be upheld because the delay in reporting the conviction was solely due to the court clerk's office, not PennDOT, and PennDOT lacks statutory authority to suspend a license until it receives a certified record.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Commonwealth Court's order, which had rescinded the operating privilege suspension for Stephen Middaugh.
